title: A filename that ends in ".exe" can display as if it ends in ".png"
assumption: What a filename's extension check says and what a user sees when they look at the filename are the same thing.

input.display: "invoice\u202egnp.exe" (RIGHT-TO-LEFT OVERRIDE, U+202E, inserted before the reversed tail "gnp.exe")
input.description: An email attachment or download named by an attacker to look safe: a real file ending in a blocked extension, disguised by an embedded bidi control character.

what_goes_wrong: name.endswith(".exe") is True — the raw string genuinely ends in ".exe" and a naive extension blocklist correctly flags it — but when this exact string is rendered by an OS file browser, email client, or terminal that honors bidi control characters, everything after U+202E is displayed right-to-left, so "gnp.exe" is painted in reverse as "exe.png": a human looking at the file sees what appears to be a harmless PNG, not the executable the code just correctly identified.
why: U+202E (RIGHT-TO-LEFT OVERRIDE) is a Unicode bidirectional formatting control: it tells a bidi-aware renderer to lay out everything that follows as if it were right-to-left text, purely for display, with no effect on the underlying code point sequence or on any string method. This is the classic "Unicode RLO" spoof used to disguise malware extensions in the wild: the code's view of the string (and any endswith/regex check on it) is accurate and unaffected, which is precisely why the attack works on humans rather than on code — the mismatch is between what is stored and what a bidi-rendering surface draws, not a parsing bug.
fix: Strip or reject Unicode bidirectional format characters (U+202A-U+202E, U+2066-U+2069) from filenames and other security-relevant display strings at the point of upload/creation, and never trust a rendered filename's apparent extension — always resolve the extension from the raw code point sequence.

sources.title: Unicode Standard Annex #9: Unicode Bidirectional Algorithm

test_cases.note: their_function(name, ext) checking name.endsWith(ext) correctly returns true on the raw string — the vulnerability is that a human reading the rendered name will disagree with this correct answer.
